'''Millie Elizabeth Hughes-Fulford''' ({{née}} '''Hughes'''; December 21, 1945 – February 2, 2021) was an American medical investigator, molecular biologist, and [[payload specialist]] who flew aboard the [[NASA]] [[Space Shuttle Columbia|Space Shuttle ''Columbia'']] in June 1991.<ref name="collect"/>

== Early life ==
Millie Elizabeth Hughes was born in [[Mineral Wells, Texas]] on December 21, 1945.<ref>{{cite web |last=Pearlman |first=Robert Z. |title=Millie Hughes-Fulford, NASA's first female payload specialist in space, dies at 75 |url=https://www.space.com/astronaut-millie-hughes-fulford-obituary |website=Space.com |date=February 5, 2021 |access-date=February 7, 2021}}</ref><ref name="nyt">{{cite web|title=Millie Hughes-Fulford, NASA Shuttle Scientist, Dies at 75|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/02/11/science/space/millie-hughes-fulford-dead.html|work=The New York Times|last=Sandomir|first=Richard|date=February 11, 2021|access-date=February 12, 2021}}</ref><ref name="collect">{{cite web|url=http://www.collectspace.com/news/news-020421a-millie-hughes-fulford-payload-specialist-obituary.html|title=Millie Hughes-Fulford, first female payload specialist in space, dies|date=February 4, 2021|website=collectSPACE.com}}</ref> She graduated from [[Mineral Wells High School]] in 1962,<ref name="SF-obit"/> then entered [[college]] at the age of 16 and earned her [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in [[chemistry]] and [[biology]] from [[Tarleton State University]] in 1968.<ref name="UCSF"/> She then began her graduate work studying [[Gas-phase ion chemistry|plasma chemistry]] at [[Texas Woman's University]] as a [[National Science Foundation]] Graduate Fellow from 1968 to 1971 and earned her [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in 1972.<ref name="MSN-obit"/><ref>{{cite book|last=Hughes Wiley|first=Millie|url=https://primo-tc-na01.hosted.exlibrisgroup.com/permalink/f/1qrsekm/ALMA-TXWU2160742110001201 |title=Reactions of C1-C4 hydrocarbons in radio-frequency plasma ...|publisher=Texas Woman's University|year=1972|location=Denton, Texas|type=Ph.D. thesis|oclc=13905022}}</ref> From 1971 to 1972, she was also both an [[American Association of University Women]] Fellow and a [[MacArthur Foundation]] Fellow.<ref name="UCSF-endocrine">{{cite web|url=https://endocrine.ucsf.edu/people/millie-hughes-fulford|title=Millie Hughes-Fulford, PhD|website=endocrine.ucsf.edu}}</ref>

== Career ==
After earning her [[doctorate]] degree in 1972, Dr. Hughes-Fulford applied to roughly 100 jobs in academia, from which she received four replies.<ref name="SF-obit"/> This resulted in her joining the faculty of [[University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center]] in Dallas as a [[Postdoctoral researcher|postdoctoral fellow]] with [[Marvin D. Siperstein]], where her research focused on the regulation of [[cholesterol]] [[metabolism]].<ref name="JSC"/> Within a couple of years, she relocated with her laboratory to [[San Francisco]].<ref name="SF-obit"/>

In 1978, she noticed a printed recruiting advertisement calling for female [[astronauts]], which led her to apply for the space program. Out of the 8000 applicants, Hughes-Fulford was in the top 20 but did not make it into [[NASA Astronaut Group 8]].<ref name="SF-obit"/><!-- (Those who did included Sally Ride, who in 1983 would become the first American woman and known LGBTQ+ person in space on STS-7.) --> She was not deterred and continued pursuing a career in space; she was also a member of the [[Army Reserve Medical Command|U.S. Army Reserve Medical Corps]], achieving the rank of [[Major (rank)|major]] and serving from 1981 until 1995.<ref name="collect"/>

=== NASA ===
Selected into a [[payload specialist]] by [[NASA]] in January 1983, Hughes-Fulford flew in June 1991 aboard [[STS-40]] Spacelab Life Sciences (SLS 1), the first Spacelab mission dedicated to biomedical studies. SLS-1 was also the first mission to have a crew with three female members, and Hughes-Fulford was both NASA's first female payload specialist in orbit and the first representative of the [[United States Department of Veterans Affairs]] in space.<ref name="MSN-obit">{{cite web |last=Pearlman |first=Robert Z. |title=Millie Hughes-Fulford, NASA's first female payload specialist in space, dies at 75 |url=https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/technology/millie-hughes-fulford-nasas-first-female-payload-specialist-in-space-dies-at-75/ar-BB1dp5vs |website=msn.com |date=February 4, 2021}}</ref> The mission flew over 3.2 million miles in 146 orbits and its crew completed over 18 experiments during a nine-day period, bringing back more medical data than any previous NASA flight. Mission duration was 218 hours, 14 minutes and 21 seconds, or 9 days, 2 hours, 14 minutes, and 20 seconds.<ref name="JSC">{{cite web|title=Payload Specialist Astronaut Bio: Millie Hughes-Fulford (03/2014)|url=https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/hughes-fulford_millie_0.pdf |website=NASA |access-date=April 2, 2021}} {{PD-notice}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.spacedu.com/|title=Spacedu.com – Medical Achievements in Cell Technology|website=spacedu.com|access-date=September 3, 2004|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190109130654/http://www.spacedu.com/|archive-date=January 9, 2019|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.spacefacts.de/bios/astronauts/english/hughes-fulford_millie.htm|title=Astronaut Biography: Millie Hughes-Fulford|first=Joachim|last=Becker|website=spacefacts.de|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201018043006/http://www.spacefacts.de/bios/astronauts/english/hughes-fulford_millie.htm|archive-date=October 18, 2020|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Later career ===
After her space mission for NASA, Hughes-Fulford was a [[professor]] at the [[UCSF Medical Center|University of California, San Francisco Medical Center]] where she continued her research until her death in 2021. She created and directed the Hughes-Fulford Laboratory<ref name=":0">{{cite web|url=http://www.hughesfulfordlab.com/|title=Hughes-Fulford Laboratory|website=hughesfulfordlab.com|access-date=April 12, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210205125945/http://www.hughesfulfordlab.com/|archive-date=February 5, 2021|url-status=live}}</ref> at the [[San Francisco VA Medical Center]], where her research focus included [[immunology]], [[bioastronautics]], and [[oncology]].<ref name="SF-obit"/>

She was the Principal Investigator (PI) on a series of SpaceHab/Biorack experiments, which examined the regulation of [[osteoblast]] ([[bone]] cell) growth.<ref name="JSC"/> These experiments flew on [[STS-76]], in March 1996, [[STS-81]] in January 1997, and [[STS-84]] in May 1997, and studied the root causes of [[osteoporosis]] that occurs in astronauts during spaceflight.<ref name="collect"/> One experiment resulted in observations of changes in [[Anabolism|anabolic]] [[signal transduction]] in [[Micro-g environment|microgravity]].<ref name="JSC"/> A later collaborator was Dr. Augusto Cogoli of [[Zürich]], Switzerland; one experiment with Dr. Cogoli was lost in the [[Space Shuttle Columbia disaster|Space Shuttle ''Columbia'' disaster]],<ref name="JSC"/> and another experiment using technology from [[Affymetrix]] and [[reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction]] (RT-PCR) examined changes in T-cell gene induction in spaceflight on a joint NASA/ESA [[International Space Station]] mission that launched on the [[Soyuz TMA-9]] in 2006.<ref name="JSC"/>

Further studies of gene regulation and signal transduction in spaceflight were approved in January 2002 for [[Space Shuttle program|Shuttle]]/[[International Space Station|ISS]] experiments examining [[Kinase|protein kinase C]] (PKC) signal activation. She flew her most recent experiments to ISS on a [[SpaceX]] rocket in collaboration with the ISS International Laboratory, the [[European Space Agency]], and the [[National Institutes of Health]]. In those studies, she found one basis for changes in the immune system in spaceflight.<ref name="MSN-obit"/> Many of her publications are available at her laboratory web site.<ref name=":0"/>

Hughes-Fulford contributed over 120 papers and abstracts, including on bone and [[cancer]] growth regulation, and on the effect of spaceflight on the immune system at the cell molecular and systems biology level.<ref name="JSC"/> She was a member of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]], [[American Society for Gravitational Science and Biology]], [[American Society for Bone and Mineral Research]], [[American Society for Cell Biology]], [[American Society of Hematology]] and the [[Association of Space Explorers]].<ref name="JSC"/>

== Personal life ==
Hughes-Fulford was married twice. Her first marriage was to policeman Rick Wiley, with whom she had a daughter, and ended in divorce in the late 1970s. Her second marriage was in 1983 to George Fulford, a [[United Airlines]] pilot whom she met in 1981. She died in [[Mill Valley, California]], on February 2, 2021, of [[lymphoma]],<ref name="SF-obit">{{cite web |last=Whiting |first=Sam |title=Millie Hughes-Fulford, astronaut and UCSF scientist, dies at 75 |url=https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Millie-Hughes-Fulford-astronaut-and-UCSF-15928086.php |newspaper=San Francisco Chronicle |date=February 5, 2021}}</ref> which was the subject of her last research paper.<ref name="UCSF"/><ref name="nyt" />
